extraction.name: Multilingual LibriSpeech (MLS)
extraction.description: A large multilingual corpus suitable for speech research, derived from read audiobooks from LibriVox and consisting of 8 languages, including about 44.5K hours of English and a total of about 6K hours for other languages. The release also includes language models and baseline ASR models.
extraction.creator: Vineel Pratap, Qiantong Xu, Anuroop Sriram, Gabriel Synnaeve, Ronan Collobert
extraction.inLanguage: English, German, Dutch, Spanish, French, Portuguese, Italian, Polish
extraction.citeAs: Pratap, Vineel, Qiantong Xu, Anuroop Sriram, Gabriel Synnaeve, and Ronan Collobert. "MLS: A Large-Scale Multilingual Dataset for Speech Research." Preprint, December 22, 2020.
extraction.rai:dataCollection: The dataset is derived from read audiobooks from LibriVox, most of which are based on Project Gutenberg text data. The authors measured available LibriVox audiobook data using LibriVox APIs, selected 8 languages based on audiobook hours and availability of corresponding text sources, downloaded audiobooks using LibriLight data preparation tools, segmented long audio files into 10-20 second segments, generated pseudo-labels with acoustic models and language models, downloaded or manually retrieved source texts, normalized text, retrieved transcripts by matching pseudo-labels to source text, filtered candidate transcripts by WER, and created train, development, and test splits. Human verification was performed for development and test transcripts.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionType: Web API, Software Collection, Document analysis, Manual Human Curator
extraction.rai:dataCollectionMissingData: The training data is lower than the data presented from LibriVox because the authors may not have downloaded the text source for the audiobook, the candidate label may have been filtered during transcript retrieval, or samples were filtered while creating validation/test splits. They also removed books with corrupted metadata such as missing title or information about speakers and authors.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: Raw data consists of LibriVox audiobook audio and corresponding text sources from websites including Project Gutenberg, archive.org, ccel.org, hathitrust.org, and other language-specific online sources. For English, about 60K hours of audiobooks were read from four major website domains: gutenberg.org, archive.org, ccel.org and hathitrust.org.
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: Audio was downsampled from 48kHz to 16kHz and segmented into 10-20 second segments based on silence intervals detected using acoustic model inference and timestamps. Source text was split into overlapping 1250-word documents with stride 1000 words, matched to pseudo-labels using TF-IDF similarity on bigrams, aligned with Smith-Waterman alignment, and candidate transcripts were filtered out if WER with pseudo-labels was greater than 40%. Numbers in matched text were replaced with aligned words from pseudo-labels, and heuristics were used to handle hyphens and apostrophes.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: The authors performed NFKC normalization on text and removed unwanted characters such as punctuations, subscript/superscripts, emojis, and escape symbols. They removed end-of-line hyphenation and joined split words, prepared a list of valid unicode characters based on each language's orthography, and filtered characters outside this range. They also removed books with corrupted metadata, removed audios with multiple speakers, kept only the latest version for books sharing the same authors and title, and ensured each chapter of each valid book appears in only one partition.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Labels were created by generating pseudo-labels for segmented audio using beam-search decoding with a 4-gram language model on acoustic models, then retrieving the original transcript from source text by matching pseudo-labels to book transcripts. For development and test sets, human transcribers listened to the audio while looking at the transcript and corrected transcripts only when they found clear and obvious errors.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: After alignment, a candidate target label was generated for each audio segment and filtered out if the WER between the candidate transcript and pseudo-label was greater than 40%. For development and test sets, transcript quality was assessed by human verification, and the paper reports WER between generated transcript and human rated transcript for each language.
extraction.rai:machineAnnotationTools: wav2letter@anywhere, 4-gram language model beam-search decoding, TF-IDF similarity on bigrams, Smith-Waterman alignment, pdftotext, KenLM
extraction.rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: The dataset will be made freely available for anyone at http://www.openslr.org. The paper also states that pretrained models and recipes will be made available at https://github.com/facebookresearch/wav2letter. No updating timeframe or deprecation policy is described.
extraction.rai:personalSensitiveInformation: Speaker gender was labeled with a gender classifier and used to balance development and test sets. Speaker identity information is also present for splitting by speaker. The paper states that in-house data used to train segmentation acoustic models consisted of publicly shared videos and was completely de-identified, but this is not part of the MLS dataset itself.
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: The authors believe the dataset will promote open research in large-scale training of ASR systems and in multilingual ASR, and that it can also be used for Text-to-Speech research by extending LibriTTS and creating a larger multilingual version for TTS research.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: English is the most dominant language in the source data, with 44.5K hours of English and about 6K hours total for the other 7 languages. The dataset is based on read speech from audiobooks. The authors balanced speakers in gender and duration in development and test sets and used a gender classifier to label speakers. They also state that to avoid adding potential bias from human transcribing, transcribers were asked to correct only clear and obvious errors.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: The dataset covers only 8 languages selected based on audiobook hours and text availability. It is based on read audiobook speech rather than conversational speech. For other languages, automatic extraction of text sources was challenging because of diverse domains and invalid links, requiring manual approaches. Transcript generation is imperfect because pseudo-labels may not always have the correct transcription of the audio. Some data was excluded due to unavailable text sources, filtered candidate labels, corrupted metadata, multiple speakers, or split creation constraints. Polish language model decoding was negatively impacted by a 13% OOV rate.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: The dataset is suitable for speech research, especially Automatic Speech Recognition and Text-To-Speech research. It provides train, development, and test splits, as well as limited supervision training subsets including 10 hour, 1 hour, and six 10-minute sets for low-resource training benchmarks. The release also includes language model training data and pre-built language models.
